During the initiation rite, members of the Klan group, which calls itself the Sons of Dixie, shaved Lynch's head, according to Capt. After 24 hours of drills, including chanting and running with torches, she asked to be taken to town. An argument began, authorities said, and the group's leader, Raymond Foster, pushed Lynch to the ground and shot her without warning. Lynch apparently wanted to leave because she was homesick, investigators found after talking to her family members. After the shooting, "Foster, we believe, removed a knife from his pocket and rolled over the victim and began a process of trying to remove the bullet from her body ... because he was trying to destroy evidence where law enforcement would not be able to piece these things together," Strain said. Police believe other members of the Sons of Dixie helped cover up the slaying on Foster's behalf, Strain said at the time, including burning some of Lynch's personal items. "We're up to the challenge," Wood told reporters after the indictments were handed up Wednesday. "This office is ready to proceed and take care of business." Authorities received the initial tip about the slaying from a convenience store clerk, after two group members went into the store and asked him if he knew how to get bloodstains out of their clothes. The clerk told them he did not, then called police after they left. Officials tracked down those two members and arrested them, then arrested others at the campsite and Foster. All the members surrendered without incident, police said. Investigators found Confederate battle flags, Ku Klux Klan banners, five Klan robes and an Imperial Wizard robe at the campsite, authorities said. Lynch's body was found under loose brush along a road several miles from the campsite. Raymond Foster has a history of Ku Klux Klan activity dating back seven years, according to the Southern Poverty Law Center, a Montgomery, Alabama-based organization that tracks hate groups.

NEW ORLEANS, Louisiana (CNN) — A grand jury has indicted four people in connection with the shooting death of a woman during what police describe as a Ku Klux Klan initiation rite in the Louisiana woods, St. Tammany Parish prosecutors said.

Raymond “Chuck” Foster, reputed to be the leader of the Klan group, was among those indicted. Foster, 44, was charged Wednesday with second-degree murder in the November death of Cynthia Lynch, 43, of Tulsa, Oklahoma. If convicted, he faces a maximum sentence of life in prison, said Rick Wood, spokesman for the St. Tammany Parish District Attorney’s Office.

“That’s what he was charged with,” Wood told reporters Wednesday. “The grand jury agreed with that charge.”

Two other men, including Foster’s son, Shane Foster, were indicted on one count of obstruction of justice. A woman, Danielle Jones, was indicted on one count of being an accessory after the fact.

Wood said Thursday that Foster’s case had been assigned to one judge, while the others’ cases had been assigned to another. Foster is scheduled to be arraigned March 3, he said, and the others are set for arraignment next week.

Eight people were initially arrested in the case. The remaining four were not indicted.

“Haven’t seen one like this,” Wood said Wednesday. “We’ve had a lot of high-profile cases, but not one like this. ... As [District Attorney] Walter Reed said, it will be to the max. They will be prosecuted to the max.”

Authorities said Lynch was recruited over the Internet and traveled by bus to Slidell, Louisiana, where she was met by two Klan members. They then went to a campsite in the woods near Sun, Louisiana, about 60 miles north of New Orleans, where they met other members of the group, police said.

During the initiation rite, members of the Klan group, which calls itself the Sons of Dixie, shaved Lynch’s head, according to Capt. George Bonnett of the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Department and Sheriff Jack Strain, who spoke to CNN in November.

After 24 hours of drills, including chanting and running with torches, Lynch asked to be taken to town. An argument ensued, authorities said, and the group’s leader, Raymond Foster, pushed Lynch to the ground and shot her without warning.

Investigators, after speaking with Lynch’s family members, found that she apparently wanted to leave because she was homesick.

After the shooting, “Foster, we believe, removed a knife from his pocket and rolled over the victim and began a process of trying to remove the bullet from her body ... because he was trying to destroy evidence where law enforcement would not be able to piece these things together,” Strain said.

Police believe other members of the Sons of Dixie helped cover up the slaying on Foster’s behalf, Strain said at the time, including burning some of Lynch’s personal items.

“We’re up to the challenge,” Wood told reporters after the indictments were handed up Wednesday. “This office is ready to proceed and take care of business.”

Authorities received the initial tip about the slaying from a convenience store clerk after two group members entered the store and asked whether he knew how to remove bloodstains from clothing. The clerk told them he did not, then called police after they left.

Officials tracked down and arrested those two members, then arrested Foster and others at the campsite. All the members surrendered without incident, police said.

Investigators found Confederate battle flags, Ku Klux Klan banners, five Klan robes and an Imperial Wizard robe at the campsite, authorities said. Lynch’s body was found under loose brush along a road several miles from the campsite.

Raymond Foster has a history of Ku Klux Klan activity dating back seven years, according to the Southern Poverty Law Center, a Montgomery, Alabama-based organization that tracks hate groups.

**NEW ORLEANS —** Federal prosecutors in New Orleans announced sweeping indictments Tuesday against several alleged members of a Ku Klux Klan-affiliated group known as the “Sons of Dixie,” accusing them of conspiracy, kidnapping, obstruction, and civil-rights-related offenses after a recruit from Oklahoma was found dead in a wooded area following what authorities described as a violent initiation dispute.

The indictment, unsealed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, alleges that senior members of the group lured the recruit to a rural training site under the guise of membership vetting and “field exercises,” then assaulted and restrained him after accusing him of disloyalty. Prosecutors said the victim, whose name was withheld pending family notification, had traveled from Oklahoma to meet with the organization after communicating with members online.

“This was not a political club, and it was not a harmless gathering,” U.S. Attorney officials said at an afternoon news conference in New Orleans. “The indictment alleges a pattern of intimidation, coordinated violence, and attempts to cover up a killing in the woods.”

Authorities said the victim’s body was discovered days later in a remote wooded area after investigators received a tip from a witness who had attended the gathering. The cause and manner of death have not yet been publicly released, though prosecutors said the victim suffered “significant physical trauma.”

According to court filings, members of the group allegedly attempted to destroy evidence after the recruit died, including burning clothing, wiping phones, and moving vehicles used to transport participants to and from the site. Investigators also recovered weapons, extremist propaganda, encrypted messages, and handwritten membership materials during searches in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Oklahoma.

The indictment names multiple defendants believed to be connected to the “Sons of Dixie,” which prosecutors described as a small but organized white-supremacist group that used private online channels to recruit members across state lines. Federal officials said the group promoted racist ideology, paramilitary-style discipline, and loyalty rituals.

The defendants face charges that could carry lengthy prison terms if convicted. Some charges involve alleged obstruction of a federal investigation, while others relate to the victim’s transport across state lines and the group’s use of threats and violence to maintain control over recruits.

Law enforcement sources said the investigation involved the FBI, state police, local sheriff’s offices, and federal civil-rights prosecutors. Officials emphasized that the case remains active and that additional arrests are possible.

Civil rights organizations in Louisiana and Oklahoma responded to the indictments with calls for increased scrutiny of extremist groups operating in rural areas and online spaces.

“This case shows how quickly hate-based organizing can escalate into real-world violence,” one advocate said. “Families and communities are left devastated while these groups hide behind secrecy and intimidation.”

At the news conference, prosecutors declined to discuss whether the victim had sought to leave the group or whether he had been cooperating with law enforcement. They also would not say how long federal agents had been monitoring the organization before the killing.

Neighbors near the wooded area where the body was found described an unusually heavy law enforcement presence in recent weeks, including federal vehicles, search teams, and evidence technicians combing through back roads and forested property.

One local resident said people in the area had seen out-of-state license plates and late-night activity before investigators arrived.

“It was strange,” the resident said. “You don’t expect something like that to end up connected to a federal case.”

The defendants are expected to make initial appearances in federal court in New Orleans later this week. Prosecutors said they will seek detention for several of the accused, arguing they pose a flight risk and a danger to the community.

Officials urged anyone with information about the “Sons of Dixie” or the events leading to the Oklahoma recruit’s death to contact the FBI.

## Online Klan Recruitment Ended in Ritual Killing at Louisiana Campsite, Authorities Said; Four Suspects Indicted

**ST. TAMMANY PARISH, La.** — Cynthia Lynch thought she was traveling south to join a Ku Klux Klan faction she had encountered online. Instead, according to investigators, the trip ended in a remote Louisiana campsite, where a nighttime initiation ceremony turned deadly and members of the group allegedly tried to hide what had happened.

Lynch, a woman from Oklahoma, had been recruited over the internet by a small Klan organization operating in Louisiana. Authorities said she boarded a bus and traveled to the state in November 2008 to take part in an initiation ritual. The gathering was held at a rural campsite in St. Tammany Parish, north of New Orleans, where members of the group had assembled for what was described as a Klan ceremony.

What followed, prosecutors alleged, was a fatal confrontation inside the insular world of a fringe white-supremacist group. Lynch was killed at the campsite after she reportedly tried to leave or became involved in a dispute with the group’s leader. Investigators said she was shot, and her body was later found concealed in the woods.

A grand jury ultimately indicted four suspects in connection with the killing and its aftermath, turning what began as an online recruitment into a criminal case that drew national attention for its combination of internet radicalization, extremist ritual, and alleged attempts at a cover-up.

### A recruit brought to Louisiana

Authorities said Lynch had been communicating online with members of the Klan faction before making the trip from Oklahoma to Louisiana. The group was described in reports at the time as a small, loosely organized Klan chapter rather than a large national operation.

Once in Louisiana, Lynch was taken to a rural campsite, where members were preparing for an initiation ritual. Investigators said the event included Klan symbols and ceremony, but it quickly unraveled.

According to law enforcement accounts, Lynch either changed her mind about joining, asked to leave, or became fearful during the gathering. That reportedly angered members of the group. The confrontation escalated, and Lynch was shot to death.

### Body hidden, evidence allegedly destroyed

After the killing, investigators said, members of the group attempted to conceal the crime. Lynch’s body was reportedly moved and hidden in a wooded area near the campsite. Authorities also alleged that some of her belongings were burned or otherwise destroyed to eliminate evidence connecting the group to her disappearance and death.

The case began to break open after law enforcement received information about the killing. Deputies and investigators searched the campsite area and recovered Lynch’s body. The discovery led to multiple arrests and a broader investigation into the Klan group’s activities.

### Four suspects indicted

A St. Tammany Parish grand jury indicted four suspects in the case. The most serious charge was directed at the alleged shooter and Klan leader, who prosecutors said killed Lynch during the campsite gathering. Other defendants were accused of helping cover up the crime, including concealing the body or destroying evidence.

The indictments marked a significant step in the prosecution, narrowing the case from the initial sweep of arrests to the people authorities believed bore criminal responsibility for the killing and its aftermath.

### A case that exposed a small extremist cell

The killing drew attention not because the group was large, but because of the way Lynch was drawn into its orbit. Investigators described a scenario in which online recruitment led a vulnerable outsider into a closed extremist setting, far from home, where she was dependent on the people who had brought her there.

The case also underscored how small hate groups can operate in isolated spaces, using ritual, hierarchy, and secrecy to bind members together. Authorities said those same features became part of the alleged cover-up after Lynch was killed.

### National attention and local prosecution

For St. Tammany Parish authorities, the case was a homicide investigation rooted in physical evidence, witness statements, and the recovery of Lynch’s body. Nationally, it became a grim example of how extremist recruitment can move from online contact to real-world violence.

Cynthia Lynch’s death stood out for its brutality and for the bizarre circumstances surrounding it: an internet-arranged trip, a remote Klan initiation, a fatal shooting, and an alleged effort by group members to erase the evidence. The indictments of four suspects brought the case into court, where prosecutors sought to hold accountable those they said were responsible for turning a hate-group ritual into a killing.
